tasks.title: Earth and Moon
tasks.statement: The photo of the Earth and the Moon is taken from an artificial satellite of the Earth. Estimate the stellar magnitude of the Moon for an observer on this satellite.

parts.question: Estimate the stellar magnitude of the Moon for an observer on this satellite.
parts.reference: Let us find the distance from the satellite to the Moon. Let p, R and L are angular radii as seen from the satellite (radii and distances to the Earth (E) and Moon (M)). From the equations: R_E = L_E * p_E, R_M = L_M * p_M one can find L_M / L_E = (R_M / R_E) * (p_E / p_M) or R_E / L_M = (R_E / R_M) * (p_M / p_E). The close positions of the Earth and the Moon on the picture shows us that the satellite, the Earth and the Moon are approximately on one line and therefore we can approximately say L_M = L_{EM} + L_E, or L_E = L_M - L_{EM}, where L_{EM} is the distance from the Earth to the Moon. L_M * (R_E / R_M) * (p_M / p_E) = L_M - L_{EM}, L_M = L_{EM} / (1 - (R_E / R_M) * (p_M / p_E)). From the picture we see that for the observer on the satellite the phase of the Moon is full moon. If m_p is the magnitude of the full moon for the observer on the Earth (the distance to the Moon is L_{EM}), the magnitude for the observer on the satellite is m_s = m_p + 5 \lg(L_M / L_{EM}) = m_p - 5 \lg(1 - (R_E / R_M) * (p_M / p_E)). We may measure values p_E and p_M on the picture and take values R_M, R_E and m_p (and, by the way, L_{EM}) from the table of the Solar System. p_E / p_M = 80/13 = 6.15, L_{EM} = 384400 km, R_E / R_M = R_E / D_M = 12756 km / 3475 km = 3.67, m_p = -12.7^m. m_s = -12.7^m - 5^m \lg(1 - 3.67 * 0.16) = -12.7^m - 5^m \lg(0.41) = -12.7^m + 1.9^m = -10.8^m. Measuring of p_E, p_M and correct calculations have to result to answers from -10.6^m to -11.0^m.

tasks.title: Sidereal period
tasks.statement: Estimate (at least roughly) the smallest and the largest possible orbital sidereal periods of bodies (any bodies, including artificial ones) of our Solar System.

parts.question: Estimate the smallest and the largest possible orbital sidereal periods of bodies of our Solar System.
parts.reference: The smallest sidereal period is a period of rotation of a body around a body of the Solar System with the largest mean density inside the sphere of orbit, T = 2\pi r / V = 2\pi r / (GM/r)^{1/2} = 2\pi r / (G (4/3)\pi r^3 \rho)^{1/2} = (3\pi / G\rho)^{1/2}. The densest bodies in our Solar System are located not far from the Sun. They are planets of the Earth group. The Earth has a little larger density but the orbit cannot lie near the planet surface. And the orbit around Mercury can lie just near the planet surface. As a result, the mean density inside the sphere of orbit around Mercury is equal to the density of substance, i.e. 5430 kg/m^3. T [around Mercury] = (3\pi / G\rho)^{1/2} = 5100 sec = 85 min. (Note for jury: Some students will take into account only bodies rotating around the Sun. 1 pt difference recommended, the answer for the minimal T for bodies rotating around the Sun is about 10000 sec = 167 min). The largest sidereal period is a period of rotation around the Sun of a body with the maximum possible semiaxis. We may propose roughly that the largest possible semiaxis is less than a half distance to the nearest stars, i.e. about 0.6 pc = 120000 a.u. T [in years] = (a [in a.e.])^{3/2}. T [maximum] = (120000)^{3/2} = 40 mln. years. (The semiaxis used in solutions may be in the interval 100000 - 200000 a.u., so the correct answers are 30 - 90 mln. years).

tasks.title: Mars set
tasks.statement: Estimate (at least roughly) the duration of Mars disk set for an observer at the mountain Koshka in Simeiz for Mars in Great opposition.

parts.question: Estimate the duration of Mars disk set for an observer at the mountain Koshka in Simeiz for Mars in Great opposition.
parts.reference: From the table of Solar System we may find the distance to Mars in the Great opposition S = a_M(1 - e_M) = 57.1 mln. km and the angular size of the disk of Mars, in radians \alpha = D_M / S = 6794 / 57100000 = 1.19 * 10^{-4} rad, in arcminutes \alpha_\alpha = 1.19 * 10^{-4} rad * 3438 arcmin/rad = 0.41 arcmin. Mars is near the ecliptic, this part of the sky is moving with the angular speed \omega = 360 * 60 arcmin / 86164 sec = 0.25 arcmin / sec. Taking into account that the latitude of the Simeiz is \varphi = 45^\circ, the duration of Mars disk set is \tau = \alpha / (\omega \sin \varphi) = 2.3 sec. Refraction and the height of the observer above the sea level do not affect on this value. They vary the time of the Marsset but not its duration.

tasks.title: Photo
tasks.statement: In the photo given to you there is an airplane with the Moon in the background. Let us suppose that the photo was taken in Simeiz at the day of a solar eclipse (or at one of the days closest to a solar eclipse).

parts.question: Estimate how long later is (or how long time ago was) the solar eclipse. Will it be (or was it) possible to observe this eclipse in Simeiz?
parts.reference: At first, the character of illumination of the exhaust trail from an airplane shows us that the photo was taken around the sunrise or sunset. Second, we see the illuminated area on the right side of moon. For the northern hemisphere it means that the phase of Moon is rising, i.e. the image was shot around sunset. Also it means that the new moon was a short time ago. That is, the solar eclipse already took place. (Answer: «Было - Was»). We see the illuminated area on the moon with relative size b/R about 2 mm / 52 mm. b/R = 1 - \cos \varphi, \varphi = \arccos(1 - b/R) = 15.9^\circ. (Or \varphi = (2b/R)^{1/2} = (0.077)^{1/2} = 0.277 rad = 15.9^\circ). Taking into account that the relative angular speed of the moon relative to the sun is 360^\circ / 29.534 days = 12.2^\circ per day, we may estimate the period since the new moon (solar eclipse) as 15.9^\circ / 12.2^\circ = 1.30 days = 31^h. Since the photo has been shot near sunset, this interval allows us to say that the solar eclipse definitely took place in daytime on the previous day. So it was seen in Simeiz in the case the eclipse zone covered Simeiz. (Answer: «Может быть - May be»).

tasks.title: Visit
tasks.statement: Extraterrestrial animals (animaloids) decided to colonize the Earth. The navigation devices of the spacecrafts of vituloids (lat. vitulus = seal = тюлень) needs that sometimes after the landing the Polar star (at 2^\circ 32' \delta = 89^\circ 16' at the epoch of starting the colonization) must be exactly in Zenith and the devices of crocodiloids needs that sometimes the Polar Star must be exactly on the Horizon. The devices are placed on the top of the spacecrafts and these can land on the Earth only in vertical positions. Also every device has to be invisible directly for the device of any other spacecraft. Estimate, how many spacecrafts of every type of animaloids can land on the Earth. Consider the Earth to be spherical, the spacecrafts' bottoms to be on its surface (may stay either on ground or on the water) and the height of every spacecraft is h = 0 m [Note: Task 5 in Group B has h = 10 m].

parts.question: Estimate, how many spacecrafts of every type of animaloids can land on the Earth (for h = 10 m from Group B text).
parts.reference: At first we have to find the minimum distance D between two spacecrafts. From the equation R_E^2 + L^2 = (R_E + h)^2, where R_E is the Earth's radius, we may find the distance L to the visible horizon from the top of the spacecraft, L = (2 R_E h)^{1/2} = 11.3 km. The minimum distance between two spacecrafts equals to double of this distance, i.e. D = 2L = (8 R_E h)^{1/2} = 22.6 km. The navigation devices of the spacecrafts of vituloids should stay at the circle with latitude exactly equal to the declination of the Polar Star, i.e. \varphi = 89^\circ 16'. The length of this circle is S = 2\pi \sin(90^\circ - \varphi) R_E = 512 km. So an estimate of the possible number of vituloids spacecrafts is the largest integer number not exceeding S/D = 2\pi \sin(90^\circ - \varphi) R_E / (8 R_E h)^{1/2} = 22.7. Thus, N_v = [S/D] = 22. And the navigation devices of the spacecrafts of crocodiloids should stay not at the circle but in whole belt near equator. The length of this belt is about the equator length, i.e. A = 2\pi R_E = 40076 km, and the width of the belt is twice the value \sin(90^\circ - \varphi) R_E, B = 2 \sin(90^\circ - \varphi) R_E = 163.3 km. Been placed in triangular net, calculations give: ([B/(D \sqrt{3} / 2)] + 1) \times [A/D] = 9 \times 1774 = 15966, ([B/D] + 1) \times [A/(D \sqrt{3} / 2)] = 8 \times 2048 = 16384. The second number is larger so it should be taken as the answer. Answers: 22 spacecrafts of vituloids and 16 384 spacecrafts of crocodiloids.
